title: Technical deep dive: multi-region routing & failover
summary: Deep technical session on designing multi-region routing and failover for Redwood-based inference. Covered routing policies (latency/cost/capacity), cache replication constraints, failover playbooks, routing affinity, and implications for batching/latency and quantized model fallbacks. Action items: share whitepaper, run cross-region benchmark, produce DR checklist and runbook for Acme PoC.
next_steps: Redwood to share multi-region routing whitepaper and architecture diagram (Maya)
Acme to provide representative traffic profile and golden prompts for benchmarks (Jordan)
Schedule a 2-hour benchmarking session with Redwood infra (Liam + Marco) week of 2026-05-18
Redwood to provide security & VPC onboarding checklist and required network ports
action_items: Maya Patel: share multi-region routing whitepaper by 2026-05-12
Liam Chen: prepare cross-region benchmark plan and test harness by 2026-05-16
Jordan Reyes: export 48hr production traffic sample and golden prompt set by 2026-05-14
Priya Singh: confirm VPC peering/firewall constraints and send network diagram by 2026-05-13
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to go deep on multi-region routing and failover, kind of the how and the trade-offs.
[00:10] Jordan Reyes: yeah thanks Maya, this is Jordan from Acme. main driver for us is global latency SLA during traffic spikes and also a strict DR runbook requirement from compliance.
[00:22] Liam Chen: cool, I'll start with an overview. so there are three common routing policies we recommend: latency-based (route to lowest p90 across regions), capacity-aware (route to region with available reserved capacity), and cost-weighted (prefer cheaper region unless latency degrades). in practice we run a hybrid.
[00:40] Marco Alvarez: when you say capacity-aware, do you mean you reserve in dedicated or you have dynamic scaling? our worry is sudden region loss and shard imbalance.
[00:50] Liam Chen: good question. for Dedicated customers you can provision reserved pools per region, and Redwood can do overflow routing to other regions with capacity tags. for Hosted, we use policy flags: prefer primary region, fallback tier-1 region, then tier-2. overflow is rate-limited and we use circuit-breakers to avoid cascading.
[01:12] Priya Singh: how do you handle KV cache for long-running conversations? if a user is routed to different region mid-conversation, we lose KV.
[01:20] Liam Chen: right. KV consistency is the trickiest part. options: 1) sticky routing (session affinity) so conversation sticks to same region - simplest but reduces failover granularity; 2) active-active KV replication across regions - we support eventual replication but it's high-cost and adds latency for writes; 3) prefix-level routing where short-term KV is kept in regional cache and long-term context stored centrally in customer-owned store (S3/RDS) with cold fetches.
[01:45] Jordan Reyes: active-active sounds expensive. what about snapshotting KV to a central store asynchronously? on failover you could replay last snapshot.
[01:54] Liam Chen: exactly what some customers do - periodic checkpoints for sessions. in our recommended DR playbook we snapshot KV every N requests or every M minutes depending on latency needs. restores add a small cold-start latency but keep correctness.
[02:10] Maya Patel: maybe I'll pause - the high level DR playbook we propose: detect region degradation (health probes + provider signals), initiate controlled failover: step down routing weights, enable sticky affinity TTL to avoid thrash, start capacity-aware routing to fallback, and if necessary, bring up quantized model variants in fallback region to increase throughput.
[02:32] Marco Alvarez: can you expand on "quantized model variants"? we have strict quality gates.
[02:36] Liam Chen: sure - we maintain model variants (fp16, int8 quantized, and a few tuned small-weights) and a compatibility matrix. fallback region can spin up a quantized variant with lower GPU memory and higher throughput. but you need evals: we recommend A/B checks with golden prompts during failover to validate output quality before widening traffic.
[02:56] Priya Singh: that makes sense. how fast is spin-up?
[03:00] Liam Chen: cold spin-up for a new variant is typically 30-90s on Dedicated pools if GPUs are available, faster if pre-warmed. that's why we recommend pre-warming at low capacity for standby variants if you have tight SLAs.
[03:12] Jordan Reyes: what's the network impact for replicating KV? do we need cross-region peering?
[03:17] Liam Chen: cross-region replication means egress traffic and potentially peering/VPN. for Private/VPC deployments we support VPC peering or direct connect for lower latency and secure traffic. for hosted we encrypt in transit and recommend customer-managed VPC with private endpoints.
[03:33] Marco Alvarez: on failover detection, are you using active health checks only? what about provider-side events?
[03:39] Liam Chen: both. we ingest provider events (zone fail, degraded host) and combine them with our synthetic probes and real-request latencies. we use a policy engine with thresholds: if p95 > X ms and error rate > Y for Z minutes, trigger a canary failover.
[03:56] Maya Patel: and there's also manual override for the customer and an audit trail in the console for every failover, which our security team likes.
[04:04] Priya Singh: audit logs are a must for us. does the private control plane keep full request logs?
[04:10] Liam Chen: we store metadata and traces in the control plane; payloads can be optionally logged based on retention and redaction rules. for Private deployments you can keep logs on-prem or in your cloud account.
[04:21] Jordan Reyes: let's talk about routing affinity TTLs and session stickiness, because we do a lot of short sessions and some long ones. what do you recommend?
[04:29] Liam Chen: common pattern: 5-15 minute sticky TTL for chat sessions reduces KV misses while allowing rebalancing. you can have adaptive TTLs: longer for long-running sessions detected by activity. Also you can set route affinity at customer ID level vs session ID level.
[04:45] Marco Alvarez: what about batching? if you route to different regions, batching efficiency drops.
[04:50] Liam Chen: yes. batching is very sensitive. we expose batch sizing controls per route and per priority. region-splitting can fragment batches. strategies: route similar latency/seq-length traffic to same region to maximize batching; use intelligent request coalescing at edge; or accept throughput drop and scale more. We also recommend prefix-caching to reduce tokens per request which helps latency and batching simultaneously.
[05:14] Jordan Reyes: any hard numbers for throughput delta when traffic is split across regions?
[05:18] Liam Chen: it varies a lot - we saw up to 20-35% throughput reduction if batchable traffic is split evenly across two regions versus consolidated. quantized variants can offset this by 2-3x throughput gains per GPU but watch quality.
[05:32] Priya Singh: regression detection during failover - how quick can we detect a quality drop?
[05:36] Liam Chen: with golden prompts and a small sample rate, you can detect regressions in minutes. we suggest 1% mirrored traffic to a canary variant and compute similarity metrics; if similarity drops beyond threshold, auto-roll back.
[05:51] Maya Patel: I want to touch on policy routing implementation - our control plane supports route trees with weighted pools and selectors: you can write policies like: route where region==us-east and cost-tier==gold then weight 0.7 else route to fallback. Policies are evaluated at request time with caching.
[06:10] Marco Alvarez: is policy evaluation in-path or precomputed? latency concerns.
[06:13] Liam Chen: lightweight evaluation in-path (sub-millisecond) using precompiled decision tables. heavy decisions (rebalancing) run asynchronously.
[06:20] Jordan Reyes: and for on-prem/private, how does the control plane talk to your runtime?
[06:24] Liam Chen: Private has an agent-based control plane connector: signals are pushed only, and we support air-gapped mode where the control plane is customer-hosted. Secrets and keys never leave customer's KMS unless explicitly permitted.
[06:36] Priya Singh: if a region is down, do you switch client IPs or do you change DNS? what's the recommended pattern?
[06:41] Liam Chen: we avoid relying solely on DNS TTLs for fast failover. recommended is edge-level routing (CDN or global LB) where we update routing weights and edge does quick re-route. DNS-based fallback is slower and subject to caching. For strict SLA, put a global LB in front and keep short TTL plus health checks.
[06:59] Marco Alvarez: we use CloudFront + ALB, would that integrate?
[07:02] Liam Chen: yes, we have reference patterns for CloudFront with Lambda@Edge to steer to region-specific endpoints, or using global LBs with origin failover. we'll share the diagrams.
[07:12] Jordan Reyes: let's talk about cost controls during failover. if we suddenly route to expensive region, can we cap spend?
[07:18] Maya Patel: yes, Redwood has cost-based routing caps: you can set hard spend caps that trigger degraded mode (lower model quality or rate-limits) instead of unconstrained failover.
[07:29] Priya Singh: nice. what about SLOs during failover? do you publish expected degradation?
[07:33] Liam Chen: our guidance: expect a transient latency spike and potential quality delta when switching to quantized fallbacks. If pre-warmed variants are available, you get under 2x latency increase; otherwise cold starts up to 90s plus throughput drop.
[07:48] Marco Alvarez: what would you recommend as our PoC setup?
[07:51] Liam Chen: start with a primary region (us-east), a tier-1 fallback (us-west) with reserved capacity sized for 30-50% of peak, and a tier-2 (eu-west) for cost offload. implement session sticky TTL 10min, enable snapshotting every 2 minutes, pre-warm int8 variant at 5% standby capacity, and mirror 1% traffic to canary during failover.
[08:15] Jordan Reyes: ok sounds good. a couple of security Qs: network egress costs and encryption, and also how audit logs are retained for Private.
[08:24] Maya Patel: we'll include a VPC onboarding doc with port list and encryption details. for Private you can set log retention and stubs for SIEM integration.
[08:33] Priya Singh: any gotchas for our infra? we have strict egress controls and only specific peering allowed.
[08:38] Liam Chen: we can do a hybrid: keep control plane signaling minimal over a single outbound port and tunnel to your peered endpoint. data paths for KV replication can be routed over your private backbone. We'll provide a recommended firewall rule set.
[08:52] Jordan Reyes: great. last thing: runbook checklist for DR?
[08:56] Maya Patel: quick recap of the DR checklist we'll put in the runbook: detect -> notify -> snapshot KV -> switch routing weights -> pre-warm fallbacks -> monitor golden prompts -> validate outputs -> rollback if regression -> postmortem. We'll attach timelines and ownership.
[09:14] Marco Alvarez: perfect. thanks.
[09:17] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, action items as discussed we'll share the paper and schedule benchmarks.
[09:22] Jordan Reyes: thanks Maya, Liam, Priya, Marco.
[09:25] [meeting ends]
